sectionTitle: Solar system; stability of orbital motions; satellites (physics only)

specStatements.text: Within our solar system there is one star, the Sun, plus the eight planets and the dwarf planets that orbit around the Sun. Natural satellites, the moons that orbit planets, are also part of the solar system.
Our solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy.
The Sun was formed from a cloud of dust and gas (nebula) pulled together by gravitational attraction.
Students should be able to explain:
• how, at the start of a star's life cycle, the dust and gas drawn together by gravity causes fusion reactions
• that fusion reactions lead to an equilibrium between the gravitational collapse of a star and the expansion of a star due to fusion energy.
A star goes through a life cycle. The life cycle is determined by the size of the star.
Students should be able to describe the life cycle of a star:
• much more massive than the Sun.
Fusion processes in stars produce all of the naturally occurring elements. Elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova.
The explosion of a massive star (supernova) distributes the elements throughout the universe.
Students should be able to explain how fusion processes lead to the formation of new elements.
Gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites (both natural and artificial) to maintain their circular orbits.
Students should be able to describe the similarities and distinctions between the planets, their moons, and artificial satellites.
(HT only) Students should be able to explain qualitatively how:
• (HT only) for circular orbits, the force of gravity can lead to changing velocity but unchanged speed
• (HT only) for a stable orbit, the radius must change if the speed changes.

concepts.definition: One star, the Sun, together with the eight planets and the dwarf planets that orbit around the Sun, plus the natural satellites (moons) that orbit those planets.
A large body in orbit around the Sun. There are eight planets in our solar system.
A smaller body that orbits the Sun and is counted as part of the solar system but is not one of the eight planets.
A moon: a body that orbits a planet rather than orbiting the Sun directly. Natural satellites are part of the solar system.
A body, such as the Sun, in which fusion reactions release energy. Our solar system contains exactly one star.
The galaxy that contains our solar system. Our solar system is only a small part of it.
A cloud of dust and gas in space. The Sun was formed from a nebula pulled together by gravitational attraction.
The attractive force between masses. It is the force that pulls the dust and gas of a nebula together to begin a star.
The hot, dense body formed as gravity pulls a cloud of dust and gas together, before fusion reactions begin.
A reaction in which small nuclei join to form a larger nucleus, releasing energy. Fusion begins once gravity has made a protostar hot and dense enough.
The balance in a stable star between the gravitational collapse pulling it inwards and the expansion caused by the energy released by fusion.
The long, stable stage of a star's life during which the inward gravitational collapse and the outward expansion due to fusion energy are in equilibrium.
The sequence of stages a star passes through. Which sequence a star follows is determined by the size of the star.
The stage a star about the size of the Sun swells into when it leaves the main sequence.
The small, dense remnant left when a red giant of about the Sun's size collapses at the end of its life.
The cold, non-luminous remnant a white dwarf becomes once it has cooled down completely.
The stage a star much more massive than the Sun swells into when it leaves the main sequence.
The explosion of a massive star. It produces the elements heavier than iron and distributes all the elements throughout the universe.
The extremely dense remnant left at the centre after a supernova.
The remnant left after the supernova of the most massive stars, whose gravity is so strong that light cannot escape.
Fusion processes in stars produce all of the naturally occurring elements; elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova.
A man-made object placed in orbit around a planet, held in that orbit by gravity in the same way as a moon.
A path around a larger body in which the distance from that body stays the same, maintained by the force of gravity.
Speed is how fast something moves; velocity is speed in a stated direction. A change of direction alone changes the velocity.
An orbit that repeats indefinitely. For a stable orbit the radius must change if the orbital speed changes.

misconceptions.question: Are dwarf planets and moons part of the solar system?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The solar system is the Sun, the eight planets, the dwarf planets and the moons that orbit the planets.
misconceptions.misconception: The solar system is only the Sun and the eight planets; dwarf planets and moons are separate things nearby.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Primary-school posters show a Sun and eight planets in a row, so anything missing from that picture is not counted as a member.
misconceptions.correction: The specification lists the members as one star, the eight planets, the dwarf planets, and the natural satellites that orbit planets. All of them belong.

misconceptions.question: Is the Sun a planet or a star?
misconceptions.correct: The Sun is a star, and it is the only star in our solar system.
misconceptions.misconception: The Sun is just a very large, very hot planet at the centre.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The Sun is drawn in the same diagram as the planets and looks like one more circle, and students rarely see it grouped with other stars.
misconceptions.correction: A star releases energy by fusion reactions in its core; a planet does not. The Sun is the one star of the solar system.

misconceptions.question: How many planets orbit the Sun?
misconceptions.correct: Eight. Pluto is classified as a dwarf planet, not one of the eight planets.
misconceptions.misconception: Nine, because Pluto is still one of the planets.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Older books, songs and mnemonics learned before 2006 still list nine planets.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that the solar system has eight planets plus dwarf planets. Pluto is one of the dwarf planets.

misconceptions.question: What does a natural satellite orbit?
misconceptions.correct: A natural satellite (a moon) orbits a planet.
misconceptions.misconception: A natural satellite orbits the Sun directly, like a small planet.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that everything in the solar system 'goes round the Sun' and apply that to moons as well.
misconceptions.correction: Moons orbit planets; the planets in turn orbit the Sun. That is why moons are called natural satellites of their planet.

misconceptions.question: How does our solar system relate to the Milky Way?
misconceptions.correct: Our solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy.
misconceptions.misconception: The Milky Way is inside our solar system, or is another name for it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both words describe 'everything out there' in casual use, so the scale difference between them is never registered.
misconceptions.correction: A galaxy is a huge collection of many billions of stars. The Milky Way contains our solar system, not the other way round.

misconceptions.question: Is the Milky Way the whole universe?
misconceptions.correct: No. The Milky Way is one galaxy among a great many in the universe.
misconceptions.misconception: The Milky Way galaxy is the entire universe.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The Milky Way is the only galaxy most students can name, so it becomes a stand-in for everything.
misconceptions.correction: The universe contains billions of galaxies. The Milky Way is simply the one that our solar system sits in.

misconceptions.question: What force pulls a nebula together to start a star?
misconceptions.correct: Gravitational attraction pulls the dust and gas of the nebula together.
misconceptions.misconception: Magnetic attraction, or the push of surrounding pressure, squeezes the cloud together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Magnetism is the attraction students meet most often in the lab, and 'squeezing' feels more active than a pull.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that the Sun formed from a cloud of dust and gas (nebula) pulled together by gravitational attraction.

misconceptions.question: Why does a protostar become hot enough for fusion?
misconceptions.correct: Gravity pulls the dust and gas closer together, and the material heats up as it is compressed.
misconceptions.misconception: The cloud catches fire and burns chemically, like a very large fuel supply.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday word 'burning' is used for the Sun, which suggests a chemical reaction with a fuel.
misconceptions.correction: No chemical burning takes place. Gravitational collapse raises the temperature and density until nuclei fuse.

misconceptions.question: Does fusion begin as soon as a cloud starts to collapse?
misconceptions.correct: No. Gravity must first compress and heat the material until it is hot and dense enough for fusion.
misconceptions.misconception: Fusion starts the moment gravity begins drawing the dust and gas together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The life cycle is taught as a list of stages, so the gap between 'gravity pulls' and 'fusion starts' is easy to miss.
misconceptions.correction: Fusion needs extreme temperature and pressure. These are produced by the gravitational collapse, so collapse comes first.

misconceptions.question: What is in equilibrium in a stable star?
misconceptions.correct: The gravitational collapse of the star inwards balances the expansion of the star caused by fusion energy.
misconceptions.misconception: Equilibrium means that no forces are acting on the star at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Balanced' is heard as 'nothing happening', so students picture a star with the forces switched off.
misconceptions.correction: Equilibrium means the inward and outward effects are equal and opposite, so the star stays the same size. Both are still acting.

misconceptions.question: What balances gravity in a main sequence star?
misconceptions.correct: The expansion caused by the energy released in fusion reactions balances the gravitational collapse.
misconceptions.misconception: Gravity itself pushes outwards as well as pulling inwards, so it balances itself.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know gravity is the only named force in the topic, so they make it do both jobs.
misconceptions.correction: Gravity acts inwards only. The outward effect comes from the energy released by fusion in the core.

misconceptions.question: What determines the life cycle a star will follow?
misconceptions.correct: The size (mass) of the star determines its life cycle.
misconceptions.misconception: The colour or surface temperature of the star determines its life cycle.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Colour is the most visible property of a star, so it is assumed to be the property that matters.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that the life cycle is determined by the size of the star. Mass decides which path a star takes.

misconceptions.question: What happens to a star about the size of the Sun after the main sequence?
misconceptions.correct: It swells into a red giant, then collapses to a white dwarf, which cools to a black dwarf.
misconceptions.misconception: It explodes as a supernova at the end of its life.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The supernova is the dramatic ending everyone remembers, so it gets applied to every star.
misconceptions.correction: Only stars much more massive than the Sun explode as supernovae. A Sun-sized star ends as a white dwarf.

misconceptions.question: Where does the red giant stage come in the life cycle?
misconceptions.correct: After the main sequence stage, when the star leaves the main sequence.
misconceptions.misconception: Before the main sequence, because a young star must be large first.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate 'giant' with the early growth of the star from a big cloud rather than with its old age.
misconceptions.correction: The order is protostar, then main sequence star, then red giant. The giant stage belongs to the end of the star's life.

misconceptions.question: What is left after the supernova of a massive star?
misconceptions.correct: A neutron star, or a black hole if the star was massive enough.
misconceptions.misconception: Every supernova leaves a black hole behind.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Black holes are the best-known object linked to dying massive stars, so they are assumed to be the only outcome.
misconceptions.correction: A supernova leaves a neutron star; only the most massive stars leave a black hole.

misconceptions.question: Which is larger, a red giant or a white dwarf?
misconceptions.correct: The red giant is far larger; the white dwarf is the small dense remnant left when it collapses.
misconceptions.misconception: The white dwarf is a large bright star that forms before the red giant stage.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'white' suggests hot and bright, which students equate with big and young.
misconceptions.correction: A white dwarf is very small and very dense. It is the late-stage remnant of a Sun-sized star, formed after the red giant stage.

misconceptions.question: Which elements are produced by fusion inside stars?
misconceptions.correct: Fusion processes in stars produce all of the naturally occurring elements, with elements heavier than iron produced in a supernova.
misconceptions.misconception: Only hydrogen and helium are made in stars; the rest were always present.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fusion is usually introduced with hydrogen forming helium, and students stop the story there.
misconceptions.correction: Fusion in stars builds heavier and heavier nuclei, producing all the naturally occurring elements between them.

misconceptions.question: Where are elements heavier than iron produced?
misconceptions.correct: In a supernova.
misconceptions.misconception: Fusion in ordinary stars produces only the elements heavier than iron.
misconceptions.whyItArises: If fusion makes elements, it seems natural that it makes all of them in the same place.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is specific: elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova, not in normal stellar fusion.

misconceptions.question: What does a supernova do to the elements a star has made?
misconceptions.correct: The explosion distributes the elements throughout the universe.
misconceptions.misconception: The explosion destroys the elements, breaking them back down into hydrogen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Explosion' is read as total destruction, so the material is assumed to be lost rather than scattered.
misconceptions.correction: The supernova throws the material outwards, spreading the elements through the universe where they can form new stars and planets.

misconceptions.question: What happens to nuclei in a fusion process?
misconceptions.correct: Small nuclei join together to form a larger nucleus, which is a nucleus of a different element.
misconceptions.misconception: A large nucleus splits into smaller nuclei, forming the new elements.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fusion and fission are taught close together and are easily swapped.
misconceptions.correction: Fusion joins nuclei; fission splits them. New, heavier elements form in stars because nuclei fuse.

misconceptions.question: What keeps a planet or satellite in its orbit?
misconceptions.correct: Gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites to maintain their circular orbits.
misconceptions.misconception: There is no gravity in space, so an orbiting body simply keeps drifting round.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Astronauts are seen floating, which is taken as proof that gravity has run out.
misconceptions.correction: Gravity acts over vast distances and is exactly what holds a body in orbit. Without it the body would travel in a straight line.

misconceptions.question: How do artificial satellites differ from moons?
misconceptions.correct: Artificial satellites are man-made; moons are natural. Both orbit a planet and both are held by gravity.
misconceptions.misconception: Artificial satellites are held up by their engines rather than by gravity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rockets need engines to launch, so students assume the engines must keep running to stay up there.
misconceptions.correction: Once in orbit a satellite needs no engine. Gravity supplies the force for the circular orbit, exactly as it does for a moon.

misconceptions.question: In a circular orbit, do the speed and the velocity stay the same?
misconceptions.correct: The speed stays the same but the velocity changes, because the direction of motion keeps changing.
misconceptions.misconception: Both speed and velocity stay constant, because the satellite goes round at a steady rate.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday language speed and velocity mean the same thing, so a constant rate seems to fix both.
misconceptions.correction: Velocity is speed in a given direction. In a circular orbit the direction changes continuously, so the velocity changes even though the speed does not.

misconceptions.question: In which direction does gravity act on a satellite in a circular orbit?
misconceptions.correct: Towards the centre of the orbit, at right angles to the direction the satellite is moving.
misconceptions.misconception: Along the direction of travel, so it makes the satellite go faster and faster.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students expect a force to speed things up, because that is what a force does in straight-line motion.
misconceptions.correction: The gravitational force is perpendicular to the motion in a circular orbit, so it changes the direction only, not the speed.

misconceptions.question: What must happen to the radius if an orbiting body speeds up?
misconceptions.correct: The radius must decrease: a faster stable orbit is a smaller orbit.
misconceptions.misconception: The radius must increase, because a faster body is flung further out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Whirling an object on a string, or a fairground ride, suggests that going faster throws you outwards.
misconceptions.correction: For a stable orbit, a greater speed means a smaller radius and a smaller speed means a larger radius.

misconceptions.question: Can an orbiting body change speed and keep the same radius?
misconceptions.correct: No. For a stable orbit at a given radius there is only one possible speed, so the radius must change if the speed changes.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes, a satellite can orbit at any speed it likes at a fixed radius.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Cars can be driven round the same roundabout at different speeds, and that everyday picture is carried over to orbits.
misconceptions.correction: A stable orbit requires gravity to match the circular motion exactly, so each radius allows only one orbital speed.

misconceptions.question: Where is our solar system in the Milky Way?
misconceptions.correct: It lies in one of the spiral arms, far out from the centre of the galaxy.
misconceptions.misconception: Our solar system sits at the centre of the Milky Way galaxy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams put the Sun at the middle of the page, and the Sun is already the centre of the solar system.
misconceptions.correction: The Milky Way contains many billions of stars. Our solar system is a small part of it, well away from the centre.

misconceptions.question: What holds a star up against its own gravity?
misconceptions.correct: The expansion caused by the energy released in fusion reactions.
misconceptions.misconception: An upthrust from the gas surrounding the star, as with a floating object.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Upthrust is the balancing force students meet in the forces topic, so it is reused here.
misconceptions.correction: There is no surrounding fluid to provide upthrust. The outward effect comes from the fusion energy released in the core.

misconceptions.question: Does how bright a star looks from Earth decide its life cycle?
misconceptions.correct: No. The life cycle is determined by the size of the star.
misconceptions.misconception: The brighter a star looks from Earth, the longer and more dramatic its life cycle.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Brightness in the sky is the only stellar measurement students make themselves, so it feels important.
misconceptions.correction: Apparent brightness depends mostly on distance. It is the size, or mass, of a star that determines its life cycle.

misconceptions.question: Do all stars eventually become supergiants if they live long enough?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only stars much more massive than the Sun become red super giants.
misconceptions.misconception: Every star becomes a supergiant in the end; it is just a matter of age.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The life cycle is presented as a single chart, so students read it as one path everything travels along.
misconceptions.correction: There are two paths, and which one a star takes is fixed by its size. Age moves a star along its own path only.

misconceptions.question: Do the elements made in a star stay inside it?
misconceptions.correct: No. A supernova distributes the elements throughout the universe.
misconceptions.misconception: The elements stay locked inside the dead remnant of the star for ever.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The remnant is described as what is 'left behind', which suggests everything else stayed put too.
misconceptions.correction: The supernova explosion throws the star's material outwards, spreading the elements through the universe.

misconceptions.question: Is an orbiting body held in place by an outward force?
misconceptions.correct: No. Gravity is the only force needed; it acts towards the centre of the orbit.
misconceptions.misconception: An outward force balances gravity and holds the body at a fixed distance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Being thrown outwards on a roundabout feels like an outward force, so it is assumed to exist in orbit too.
misconceptions.correction: The felt outward push is an effect of the body's own motion, not a force acting on it. Gravity alone maintains the orbit.

misconceptions.question: Which is constant in a circular orbit, the speed or the velocity?
misconceptions.correct: The speed is constant; the velocity changes because the direction changes.
misconceptions.misconception: The velocity is constant and it is the speed that keeps changing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two words are learned as a pair and their definitions are easily swapped over under pressure.
misconceptions.correction: Velocity includes direction, so it is the quantity that changes on a curved path. The speed stays the same.

mcqs.stem: Which list correctly describes what our solar system contains?

options.text: One star, the eight planets, the dwarf planets and the planets' moons
options.rationale: This is exactly the membership the specification gives: one star, the Sun, the eight planets, the dwarf planets, and the natural satellites that orbit planets.

options.text: One star and the eight planets that orbit around it, nothing else
options.rationale: A student working from the familiar Sun-and-eight-planets diagram leaves out everything that diagram omits.

options.text: One star, nine planets including Pluto, and the moons of those
options.rationale: A student who still counts Pluto as a planet gives nine rather than eight.

options.text: Eight planets and their moons, with the Sun counted as a planet
options.rationale: A student who does not accept that the Sun is a star treats it as one more body in the list.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by a natural satellite?

options.text: A small rocky body that orbits the Sun directly, between the planets
options.rationale: A student who believes everything in the solar system orbits the Sun directly puts moons in solar orbit.

options.text: A dwarf planet, which orbits the Sun beyond the eight planets
options.rationale: A student who does not distinguish the categories treats every 'extra' body as the same thing.

options.text: A moon: a body that orbits a planet rather than orbiting the Sun
options.rationale: The specification defines natural satellites as the moons that orbit planets, and states that they are part of the solar system.

options.text: A man-made craft kept in orbit by its engines, not gravity
options.rationale: Reflects the belief that artificial satellites are held up by their engines rather than by gravity (m22).

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes how our solar system relates to the Milky Way?

options.text: The Milky Way is just another name for our own solar system
options.rationale: A student who has met both terms as 'space' words treats them as interchangeable.

options.text: Our solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy
options.rationale: The specification states directly that our solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy.

options.text: The Milky Way galaxy holds everything in the universe
options.rationale: A student who can name only one galaxy assumes it is all there is.

options.text: Our solar system lies at the exact centre of the Milky Way
options.rationale: A student generalises the Sun's central position in the solar system to the galaxy as a whole.

mcqs.stem: How was the Sun formed?

options.text: From a cloud of dust and gas squeezed together by magnetism
options.rationale: A student substitutes the attraction met most often in the laboratory for gravitational attraction.

options.text: From a huge ball of chemical fuel that was set alight in space
options.rationale: A student who hears the Sun described as 'burning' pictures a chemical fire.

options.text: From a cloud of dust and gas in which fusion started at once
options.rationale: A student who learns the stages as a list misses that gravity must compress and heat the cloud first.

options.text: From a cloud of dust and gas pulled together by gravity
options.rationale: The specification states that the Sun was formed from a cloud of dust and gas (nebula) pulled together by gravitational attraction.

mcqs.stem: At the start of a star's life cycle, why do fusion reactions begin?

options.text: Gravity draws the dust and gas together, heating it until nuclei fuse
options.rationale: Gravitational attraction pulls the material of the nebula together; the compression raises the temperature and density until fusion reactions start.

options.text: The dust and gas catch fire and burn chemically, giving out the energy
options.rationale: A student who treats the Sun as a fire looks for a chemical reaction rather than a nuclear one.

options.text: Fusion starts as soon as gravity begins to draw the cloud inwards
options.rationale: A student who sees no gap between the stages assumes fusion is immediate.

options.text: Magnetic forces squeeze the cloud until its particles join together
options.rationale: A student replaces gravitational attraction with the attraction they meet in magnetism.

mcqs.stem: Which two effects are in equilibrium in a stable star?

options.text: No effects at all, because equilibrium means no forces act on it
options.rationale: A student reads 'balanced' as 'nothing happening' and switches the forces off.

options.text: The inward pull of gravity and the outward push of gravity itself
options.rationale: A student who knows only one named force in this topic makes gravity do both jobs.

options.text: The weight of the star and the upthrust of the gas around it
options.rationale: A student reuses the floating model from the forces topic where it does not apply.

options.text: The gravitational collapse inwards and the expansion due to fusion energy
options.rationale: The specification states that fusion reactions lead to an equilibrium between the gravitational collapse of a star and its expansion due to fusion energy.

mcqs.stem: A main sequence star stays the same size for billions of years. Why?

options.text: No forces act inside a star once it reaches the main sequence
options.rationale: A student who equates equilibrium with the absence of forces concludes nothing is acting.

options.text: Its inward collapse and its outward expansion stay balanced
options.rationale: While fusion continues at a steady rate, the expansion due to fusion energy exactly balances the gravitational collapse, so the star's size does not change.

options.text: Gravity pushes the star outwards as hard as it pulls it inwards
options.rationale: A student makes gravity self-balancing rather than naming the fusion energy.

options.text: The upthrust of the gas around it supports the star's weight
options.rationale: A student imports upthrust from floating, which needs a surrounding fluid that is not there.

mcqs.stem: What determines the life cycle that a star will follow?

options.text: The colour of the star, which shows its surface state
options.rationale: A student picks the most visible property of a star and assumes it is the decisive one.

options.text: How bright the star looks when viewed from Earth
options.rationale: A student uses the one stellar measurement they can make themselves, which mostly reflects distance.

options.text: The size of the star, which sets the path it takes
options.rationale: The specification states that the life cycle of a star is determined by the size of the star.

options.text: The age of the star, since all stars follow one path
options.rationale: A student who has seen a single life-cycle chart reads it as one route that every star travels.

mcqs.stem: A star about the size of the Sun leaves the main sequence. What happens next?

options.text: It explodes straight away as a supernova
options.rationale: A student applies the memorable supernova ending to every star, whatever its size.

options.text: It shrinks back to become a protostar
options.rationale: A student who places the giant stage early in the cycle expects the star to go backwards.

options.text: It becomes a white dwarf at once
options.rationale: A student who skips the red giant stage jumps to the remnant.

options.text: It expands and becomes a red giant
options.rationale: For a star of about the Sun's size, the stage after the main sequence is the red giant.

mcqs.stem: What is the full sequence of stages at the end of the life of a star about the size of the Sun?

options.text: Red giant, then white dwarf, then black dwarf
options.rationale: A star of about the Sun's size swells into a red giant, collapses to a white dwarf, and finally cools to a black dwarf.

options.text: Red giant, then supernova, then a neutron star
options.rationale: A student who expects every star to explode inserts a supernova into the Sun's path.

options.text: Red super giant, then supernova, then black hole
options.rationale: A student confuses the two branches of the life cycle and uses the massive-star path.

options.text: White dwarf, then red giant, then a black dwarf
options.rationale: A student who thinks a white dwarf is a large early stage puts the stages in the wrong order.

mcqs.stem: What happens to a star much more massive than the Sun after the main sequence?

options.text: Red giant, then white dwarf, then black dwarf, just as the Sun will
options.rationale: A student who knows only one life cycle applies the Sun's path to every star.

options.text: Red super giant, then supernova, then neutron star or black hole
options.rationale: A star much more massive than the Sun becomes a red super giant, explodes as a supernova, and leaves a neutron star or a black hole.

options.text: Red super giant, then supernova, then always a black hole
options.rationale: A student who links massive stars only with black holes forgets the neutron star outcome.

options.text: Red super giant, then protostar, then a new main sequence star
options.rationale: A student who misorders the cycle sends the star back to an early stage.

mcqs.stem: What can be left at the centre after a massive star explodes as a supernova?

options.text: A black hole, whatever the mass of the star that exploded
options.rationale: A student who associates supernovae only with black holes drops the neutron star case.

options.text: A white dwarf that later cools to become a black dwarf
options.rationale: A student who mixes the two branches uses the Sun's remnants for a massive star.

options.text: A neutron star, or a black hole if the star was massive enough
options.rationale: A supernova leaves a very dense neutron star, and for the most massive stars a black hole.

options.text: Nothing at all, as the star is completely destroyed
options.rationale: A student who reads 'explosion' as total destruction expects no remnant.

mcqs.stem: Which elements are produced by fusion processes in stars?

options.text: Only hydrogen and helium, and nothing more
options.rationale: A student stops at the hydrogen-to-helium reaction used to introduce fusion.

options.text: Only those elements that are heavier than iron
options.rationale: A student who remembers the supernova rule applies it to all stellar fusion.

options.text: All of the naturally occurring elements
options.rationale: The specification states that fusion processes in stars produce all of the naturally occurring elements.

options.text: Only elements made by the splitting of nuclei
options.rationale: A student who confuses fusion with fission describes the wrong process.

mcqs.stem: Where are the elements heavier than iron produced?

options.text: In the explosion of a massive star, a supernova
options.rationale: The specification states that elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova.

options.text: In the fusion reactions inside a main sequence star
options.rationale: A student who knows fusion makes elements assumes it makes all of them in the same place.

options.text: Nowhere; they have existed from the very start
options.rationale: A student who limits stellar fusion to helium assumes heavy elements were always present.

options.text: By the splitting of very large nuclei inside the star
options.rationale: A student who swaps fusion for fission describes nuclei breaking apart instead of joining.

mcqs.stem: What does the explosion of a massive star do to the elements it has produced?

options.text: It leaves the elements locked inside the remnant star
options.rationale: A student who focuses on what is 'left behind' assumes the material stays put.

options.text: It distributes the elements throughout the whole universe
options.rationale: The specification states that the explosion of a massive star (supernova) distributes the elements throughout the universe.

options.text: It destroys the elements, leaving only hydrogen gas
options.rationale: A student who reads 'explosion' as destruction expects the elements to be broken down.

options.text: It converts all the elements into ones lighter than iron
options.rationale: A student who half-remembers the iron rule reverses it.

mcqs.stem: How do fusion processes in stars lead to the formation of new elements?

options.text: Large nuclei split apart to form smaller nuclei of new elements
options.rationale: A student who confuses fusion with fission reverses the direction of the process.

options.text: Atoms join chemically to make new compounds and elements
options.rationale: A student who thinks of the Sun as burning describes a chemical change rather than a nuclear one.

options.text: Fusion makes only the elements heavier than iron in the core
options.rationale: A student who over-applies the supernova rule restricts fusion to heavy elements.

options.text: Small nuclei join to form larger nuclei of different elements
options.rationale: In fusion, small nuclei join to form a larger nucleus. Because the number of protons changes, the new nucleus is a nucleus of a different element.

mcqs.stem: What allows a planet or a satellite to maintain a circular orbit?

options.text: Gravity provides the force that keeps it in its circular orbit
options.rationale: The specification states that gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites, both natural and artificial, to maintain their circular orbits.

options.text: There is no gravity in space, so it just keeps drifting round
options.rationale: A student who has seen astronauts floating concludes that gravity does not act in space.

options.text: Its engines fire all the time to hold it in its orbital path
options.rationale: A student who links spacecraft with rocket engines assumes thrust is needed to stay in orbit.

options.text: An outward force balances gravity and holds it in place
options.rationale: A student who has felt thrown outwards on a ride invents an outward force acting on the body.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly compares moons and artificial satellites?

options.text: Both orbit a planet, but only the moon is held there by gravity
options.rationale: A student who thinks satellites are held up by engines denies gravity's role for them.

options.text: Both orbit a planet; moons are natural and satellites are man-made
options.rationale: Moons and artificial satellites both orbit a planet and are both held in orbit by gravity. The distinction is that moons are natural and satellites are made by people.

options.text: Both orbit the Sun directly, and both were formed with the Sun
options.rationale: A student who believes everything orbits the Sun places moons and satellites in solar orbit.

options.text: Neither one is held by gravity, since gravity does not act in space
options.rationale: A student who thinks space is gravity-free removes gravity from both cases.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) A satellite travels round a circular orbit at a steady rate. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Its speed and its velocity are both remaining constant
options.rationale: A student who treats speed and velocity as the same quantity fixes both.

options.text: Its speed keeps increasing because gravity acts upon it
options.rationale: A student who expects any force to speed a body up applies straight-line thinking to a curve.

options.text: Its speed stays the same but its velocity is changing
options.rationale: In a circular orbit gravity acts at right angles to the motion, so it changes the direction of travel and therefore the velocity, while the speed is unchanged.

options.text: Its velocity is constant but its speed is changing
options.rationale: A student who has swapped the two definitions reverses the correct answer.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) A satellite in a stable circular orbit is made to travel faster. For the orbit to stay stable, what must happen?

options.text: The radius of the orbit must become much larger
options.rationale: A student who thinks faster motion throws a body outwards increases the radius.

options.text: The radius of the orbit can stay exactly as before
options.rationale: A student who pictures a car speeding up on a roundabout keeps the radius fixed.

options.text: The orbit turns into a straight line at once
options.rationale: A student who thinks an outward force takes over expects the satellite to leave the orbit.

options.text: The radius of the orbit must get smaller
options.rationale: For a stable orbit the radius must change if the speed changes: a faster orbital speed corresponds to a smaller orbital radius.
